# Deck prompt — for Claude Design

Paste **section 2** into Claude Design as-is. Section 1 is context for you, section 3 says
where the numbers live, section 4 is the pre-flight check.

**Every figure the deck may quote lives in [`FACTS.md`](FACTS.md)**, generated by
`npm run finalize` from the deployment record and the demo run. Do not retype numbers from
memory or from this file. If Claude Design proposes a figure that is not in FACTS.md, delete
it. A judge who catches one invented number stops believing the other twelve.

---

## 1. What this deck has to do

**Audience.** BUIDL CTC 2026 Fall judges, track AI. Assume one reader is a Creditcoin or
Gluwa engineer who has read the Attestcoin docs more carefully than we have, and one is a
CertiK reviewer who will go looking for the thing we glossed over. Write for those two.

**The job of the deck**, in order:

1. The usual way cross-chain settlement gets built has a hole in it that nobody names.
2. We closed it, it runs on their chain, and here are the transaction hashes.
3. We found a hole in our own first design too, and closed that in public.

**What loses.** Opening with market size. An architecture slide prettier than the evidence
slide. No limitations slide: with this audience, naming the boundary is what makes the rest
credible.

**Length.** 13 slides, 16:9, exported to PDF.

**Hard rules.**
- Never name, describe or compare against another project entered in this hackathon. Where a
  contrast is needed, describe the *pattern*: "designs where the party who benefits is the
  only one who submits evidence". Judges who know the space fill in the reference themselves,
  and that lands better than naming anyone.
- Never write a number that is not in `FACTS.md`.
- Do not claim the system is trustless, audited or production ready. It is none of those.

---

## 2. The prompt — paste this into Claude Design

> Design a 13-slide pitch deck, 16:9, for export to PDF. The project is **ProveOut**, a
> cross-chain job escrow submitted to the BUIDL CTC 2026 Fall hackathon, track AI.
>
> **Visual direction.** Quiet, technical, editorial: closer to a well-set engineering report
> than a startup pitch. It should look like the people who made it care about being right.
> Near-white neutral ground, near-black ink, one restrained accent used only for eyebrows and
> emphasis. Semantic colour only where it means something: green for settled, red for
> refused. Sans-serif for prose, monospace for every address, hash, code fragment and number.
> Generous margins, strong left alignment, no gradients, no stock illustration, no drop
> shadows on text. Slide numbers small, bottom right.
>
> One idea per slide. If a slide needs a paragraph to explain it, the headline is wrong.
> Headlines are claims, not labels: "Inclusion is not success", never "Technical details".
>
> ---
>
> **Slide 1 — Title**
> ProveOut
> Money moves when the work is proved, and anyone can prove it failed.
> Footer: Creditcoin CC3 Testnet · Attestcoin readability · BUIDL CTC 2026 Fall, track AI
>
> **Slide 2 — The problem**
> Headline: An AI agent working across chains cannot be paid safely.
> Body: Pay first and the buyer loses the money if the work never happens. Pay after and the
> agent has no guarantee. Every existing answer inserts a third party to decide whether the
> work was done: an oracle operator, an arbiter, or the platform itself.
>
> **Slide 3 — The hole nobody names**
> Headline: Evidence that only the winner submits is not evidence.
> Body: The standard shape of a cross-chain settlement or reputation system is that the party
> who benefits watches for their own good news and submits it. A worker sees the repayment and
> posts it. A builder finishes the job and posts the receipt.
> Pull-quote, large: **Nobody posts their own failure.**
> Closing line: Such a system does not need to censor bad news. Bad news simply never arrives,
> because the only party watching has no reason to send it.
>
> **Slide 4 — What ProveOut does**
> Three numbered columns.
> 01 Freeze. The buyer locks USDC on Creditcoin against a job whose acceptance criteria are
> hashed before any work starts. The builder stakes a bond.
> 02 Prove. The outcome is emitted as an event on Ethereum Sepolia. Attestcoin proves that
> transaction on Creditcoin, receipt and logs included, in one synchronous call.
> 03 Settle. A proved completion pays the builder. A proved failure refunds the buyer and pays
> whoever carried it a bounty out of the builder's bond.
>
> **Slide 5 — The difference, in one line**
> Centred, large, the only thing on the slide:
> **`challengeFailure` is callable by any address on earth, and it pays.**
> Below, smaller: The bounty comes out of the bond of the party that failed. The party who
> stands to lose cannot suppress the outcome, because they are not the only one who can carry
> it.
>
> **Slide 6 — The gate that matters**
> Headline: Inclusion is not success.
> Code block, monospace:
> ```
> EvmV1Decoder.ReceiptFields memory receipt = ...;
> if (receipt.receiptStatus != 1)
>     revert ReceiptNotSuccessful(receipt.receiptStatus);
> ```
> Body: The precompile proves a transaction was included in a block. A reverted transaction is
> in the block too. Without this line, a builder sends a completion call that reverts, proves
> the inclusion completely honestly, and is paid for work that never happened. Every proof
> involved is genuine.
> Footer: This is the pattern Gluwa's own reference contract uses. We did not invent it. We
> refused to skip it.
>
> **Slide 7 — Architecture**
> A clean two-column diagram. No 3D, no icons beyond simple arrows.
> Left, "Ethereum Sepolia, source": `WorkOracle.sol`, reporter-gated, emitting
> `WorkCompleted(jobId, criteriaHash, builder, outputHash)` and `WorkFailed(jobId, reason)`.
> Right, "Creditcoin CC3, settlement": `SourceRegistry.sol` mapping emitter to chain key, EVM
> chain id, topic signatures and field positions; `JobEscrow.sol is ASCBase` with
> `execute(action=0)` release, `execute(action=1)` challenge open to any caller, and `refund()`
> after the deadline.
> One arrow left to right: a relayer waits for attestation, fetches the proof, submits it.
> Untrusted, and anyone can be it.
> Caption: Verification and payout happen in one Creditcoin transaction. No message queue, no
> second confirmation.
>
> **Slide 8 — Six gates**
> A dense but calm table. Columns: Gate / Check / What it stops.
> G1 · receiptStatus == 1 · a reverted call being paid as a success
> G2 · emitter is registered · anyone deploying their own oracle and draining every escrow
> G2b · proved chain id matches · the same bytecode redeployed on another attested chain
> G3 · exact topic0 and topic count · a different event settling a job
> G4 · fields read from registered positions · indexed parameters read out of `data` as plausible garbage
> G5 · query id unseen · the same proof settling twice
> G6 · within the deadline · release and refund racing on transaction ordering
> Footer: The challenge path reuses G1 to G5 and deliberately skips G6. A failure stays
> provable forever, or hiding one until the clock ran out would be a winning strategy.
>
> **Slide 9 — It runs. Here are the hashes.**
> The most important slide. Make it the most confident one.
> Four rows, monospace, each with what it proves and its full transaction hash, taken from the
> "The demo run" table in FACTS.md. Highlight row 2 visually: it is the only row that proves
> the thing nobody else proves. Row 4 is a refusal on the source chain, not on Creditcoin, and
> should be labelled as such.
> Footer: the escrow's vault inequality still holds after all of it.
>
> **Slide 10 — The bug we shipped, and shipped a fix for**
> Headline: Our first design had a hole big enough to walk through.
> Body: `WorkOracle` originally had no access control, on the reasoning that gating it would
> reintroduce the trusted operator this project exists to remove. That reasoning was wrong. A
> builder could call `reportCompleted` naming their own job and their own address, prove it
> honestly, and be paid for work that never happened. Every one of the six gates passed: they
> check *which contract* emitted a log, and none of them can check who was allowed to call it.
> The same hole let any passer-by burn an honest builder's bond.
> Closing line: There is now a named reporter set. Transaction 04 is a builder being refused
> by name, on chain, with the decoded error in FACTS.md. We would rather show you this than
> have you find it.
> Design note: this slide is a strength, not an apology. Set it with the same confidence as
> slide 9.
>
> **Slide 11 — Integration depth**
> Headline: Verified, not assumed.
> · Block Prover precompile `0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000FD2`, confirmed against the
> docs, against the shipped package constant, and by calling it.
> · `JobEscrow` inherits `ASCBase`, so the protocol's own entry point and replay guard are the
> ones in the path. The decoder is imported from the published package, never copied in.
> · Replay protection uses the protocol's query id, derived by the precompile from the verified
> Merkle path, not a caller-supplied transaction hash.
> · 97 tests, 0 failing, including a 6,144-call invariant run on the vault balance rule.
> · A live verifier on the site: paste any Sepolia transaction hash and it calls the real
> precompile and shows the result, with no wallet and nothing spent.
> Small closing note: two documentation errors found and reported during the build.
>
> **Slide 12 — What this does not do**
> Headline: The boundary, stated plainly.
> · Attestcoin proves inclusion, not exclusion. It can prove a transaction happened; it cannot
> prove none happened. ProveOut does not make hiding a failure impossible, it makes it
> detectable and expensive. That is the whole promise of the challenge mechanism.
> · The source oracle is trusted within its own scope. Whoever holds a reporter role decides
> what is provable. We narrow trust to one named contract with a named reporter set. We do not
> eliminate it, and no proof system can.
> · TestUSDC is a demo token with an open mint and no value. Testnet only, unaudited.
> · The bond ratio is a demo parameter, not a modelled economic result.
> Design this slide with the same care as slide 9. It is not an apology; it is what makes the
> rest believable.
>
> **Slide 13 — Close**
> Repeat the thesis: Money moves when the work is proved, and anyone can prove it failed.
> Then, in monospace, the links and the JobEscrow address from FACTS.md.
> Include a QR code to the live console, bottom right, small and unobtrusive.

## 3. Where the numbers come from

Open [`FACTS.md`](FACTS.md). It is generated, so it is current by construction. It carries the
live console and verify URLs, the repository URL, every contract address with its chain, the
demo run with full hashes, and the job economics including the challenger's address.

If Claude Design asks for something not in there, the answer is that we do not have it, not
that we should estimate it.

**One detail worth a sentence if there is room.** On the first deployment, the first contract
this deployer created on Sepolia and the first it created on Creditcoin landed on the *same
address*, because CREATE derives from deployer and nonce and both were identical. That is
exactly the cross-chain collision gate G2b exists to reject, demonstrated by accident on our
own first run. True, memorable, and it shows the threat model came from thinking rather than a
checklist.

## 4. How to link the repository so a judge actually looks

A URL on a slide is not a link a judge follows. In order of value:

1. **Slide 9 carries the hashes themselves**, not a link to them. A judge can paste one into
   Blockscout without leaving their seat. The hashes are the argument, not decoration.
2. **The QR code goes to the live console**, not the repository. A console shows the settled
   jobs and the vault invariant in one screen; a repository is a wall of files.
3. **Name `docs/attestcoin-integration.md` explicitly** on slide 11. Judges scoring integration
   depth want one file that answers exactly that, and telling them which file respects their
   time.
4. **The DoraHacks "Attestcoin Protocol Integration Summary" field** should be the first two
   sections of `docs/attestcoin-integration.md`, pasted, not rewritten.
5. **Mention the verify page out loud.** "You can check this yourself right now, without a
   wallet" is a stronger close than any architecture diagram.

Before submitting, **switch the repository to public**. A private repo behind a deck link is
worse than no link: it reads as though there is something to hide, and the judge cannot check
the one thing the deck is asking them to believe.

## 5. Checks before you export

- [ ] No project entered in this hackathon is named or described anywhere.
- [ ] Every number on every slide appears in `FACTS.md`.
- [ ] Slides 10 and 12 exist and are designed as carefully as slide 9.
- [ ] Transaction hashes are complete, not truncated, and copy-pasteable.
- [ ] The repository is public and its README opens with the deployment block.
- [ ] Every link resolves. Click all of them.
